In connection with the copying in Paris of documents which bear on the early history of our country, I may say that for years we had two gentlemen there, Mr. Marmette and Mr. Richard, who had chosen out documents which referred particularly to the French regime in Canada and these gentlemen reported that these documents ought to be copied and placed in our archives. A large number of such documents have been chosen, but a comparatively small proportion of them has been copied and sent out here. A certain expenditure has been made each year in this work.
Who is in charge of that ?

Mr. Tantet an officer of the French government in the Bibliotheque Frangaise has been in charge of the aetual copying work. It is considered that there is no necessity to spend further money on the selection of these documents until we have made more progress in copying those which have already been selected. Under Air. Tantet, expert coypists of the libraries in Paris are engaged in this work, which we wish to press forward more rapidly than in the past. In addition to the archives in Canada and to the records of the other departments under the control of the government, there are a very large number of important historical documents and papers scattered throughout private libraries, in some cases in the possession of private individuals, and in other cases in possession of various local historical societies. It would be impossible to get copies of these documents within any reasonable period of time, but the greater number of them are available to the public under certain restrictions, and it is proposed to publish a guide to these documents, indicating their existence, where they are to be

found and what their character is. The student of history will be able to refer to this guide which can be prepared at a comparatively small cost. One thousand dollars will be devoted to that purpose. Also, there are a large number of historical documents bearing on Canada, not only in Paris but in Great Britain as well as in Spain, Italy and other continental European countries. We wish to find out where these are, and what their nature is so as to be able from time to time to obtain copies. I think the House and the country will agree with me that this subject of the collection and preservation of our archives is one of great interest and importance, and that it is time we should take the necessary steps to secure a systematic and efficient administration of this branch of the department.

I fully agree with what has been said by the minister as to the desirability of acquiring all historic documents and data that we can possibly get to be placed in our archives for the benefit of Canada. If, however, the minister would endeavour to get the original documents which are scattered throughout the country, instead of copies of them, it would be very much better, because it is always an object on the part of the original investigator or the historical writer to consult the original documents. I am glad to know that such progress has been made and is being made with respect to the documents in Paris. I would like to know what progress is being made with respect to the documents in the record office or in the foreign office in London. At the time of confederation all the public documents of the province of New Brunswick were taken to London, and consequently those who take an interest In historical studies have been at a great disadvantage as far as New Brunswick is concerned. I think the additional amount will be well expended if it is used in collecting historical data with respect to the Dominion of Canada. Every year that passes will make it more difficult to collect that data, and the more vigorous we are in attempting to collect it now, the better it will be for the archives department and for the future writers of the history of our country.	*

I am very glad to hear what my hon. friend has said, and I quite agree with the expressions he has used. 1 would like very much to get the original documents, and whenever we can we do so to the extent of our finances, but in very many instances the owners do not wish to part with oi'iginal documents, and then we have to take copies. This is the case almost entirely in Europe. For a number of years past we have been spending about $5,000 a year on the other side of the Atlantic, of which about $1,000 has been spent in Paris and about $4,000 in London. The great bulk of the copies we have received in our archives 1 58
library here have come from London, and not from Paris. Out of three thousand volumes which we have in our archives, only 229 have come from Paris. Each of these volumes contains a number of documents, so that the three thousand volumes would represent about half a million documents. I have been myself almost startled at the figures that have been given me of the number of documents we have in our archives. There are about half a million documents there besides the bound books. A little while ago we received from the Secretary of State's Department alone over a million documents to take charge of and look after; but we had not sufficient accommodation or facilities for dealing with them. That is one reason why it is so necessary that we should have a new fireproof building where these documents could be safely stored, classified, catalogued and made available. At the present time, in the various departments, the great majority of the documents are stored away in boxes in out of the way corners and rooms and are quite inaccessible, and in many instances there does not seem to be anybody who knows what these boxes contain. We shall have to take these documents and put them in a building where they will be safe, and then classify and catalogue them. This is a part of the work to be done as soon as the new building is ready.

I had occasion three or four times to consult the archives in Ottawa and the arrangements seemed to me to be very good indeed. I was anxious, a few months ago, to get some documents respecting the early history of New Brunswick, and I went to the archives department and in a very short time got copies of just what I wanted. They had not the originals, but they had copies which had been obtained from the offices in London. Therefore, I think we ought to feel somewhat proud that we are getting along as well as we are respecting the archives of Canada.
Has the minister enlarged the distribution of the report of the archives?
The report is printed as a parliamentary blue book. It is parliament that decides the number to be printed.
I understood the minister to state two or three years ago that he was going to supply the high schools with copies of these reports ?

The printing of that report is under the control of the House of Commons, not of the department, and the number of copies to be printed is decided by parliament through the printing committee. We have no control over it. We simply have a certain number of copies supplied to us * as a department.
I understood that the minister was going to recommend a larger distribution of these reports.

If I made that agreement, It has escaped my memory. We have had a mailing list of the copies supplied to us, just as we have had a mailing list for our departmental reports, and we have always been able to meet any demands that have come to us.
Does the report show what number of documents have been copied in England or in France during the year or the expense incurred ?

We spend just a little under $5,000 each year in Europe. I have not any figures to show the number of documents copied. The people in London are engaged by the High Commissioner's officers and those in Paris are engaged by Mr. Tan-tet, an officer of the Bibliotheque Franc,-aise, and are paid at a fixed rate per folio. One of the objects in asking for this greater expenditure is to increase the number of those working in Paris and have the documents copied more rapidly.
Will the hon. minister explain the item of $1,000 on page D-31 of the Auditor General's Report, paid Wm. M. Kearns for some books ?

That was the price of some books sold by Mr. Kearns, auctioneer, for the estate of the late Hon. Louis Masson, of Montreal. We think we have made a very good bargain. There were United States purchasers bidding against us, but we were able to secure the works, and immediately afterwards were offered a very considerable sum over what we paid for them if we would allow them to go to the United States. They are works of the greatest historical interest and our experts, Messrs. Sylvaiu, Suite and Descelies, librarians, very strongly recommended us to get them even at a figure very much higher than we bought them for.
General statistics, 818,200.

There is an item concerning which I would like to ask a question. I was not here when it passed. Each member b supplied with a monthly report of the Patent Record unbound. At the end of the year we have 12 copies. Why should members not he supplied with a bound volume containing the 12 monthly reports ? I appreciate these reports very highly because 1 receive a number of inquiries concerning them every year. There is another point I would submit to the hon. gentleman. If you want to get a type written copy of the explanation of any patent, you have to pay a very high figure tor it. In Washington one has only to pay a few cents. The department would do well to make a change in this respect and follow the example set by Washington. At this moment I have in-Mr. FISHER.
quiries from the United States for copies of patents, blit the figure asked-although not too high for the amount of writing to be done-is still so much higher than that charged in the United States that It deters people from getting it.

Willi regard to members getting bound copies, we only bind three or four for tlie use of the department. We keep tlie unbound copies, and when any one makes application for a description of a patent, we use those extra copies, and tire patent examiners must have them all the time on hand for their own reference. In the United Slates the conditions are very different from what they are here. There is such a large demand there for descriptions of patents that tlie American Patent Office find it economical to print a description of every patent issued, drawings and everything. Once these are printed, copies can be supplied at a nominal figure. But here there might not be a demand for a single copy of more that one-quarter of all the patents issued in a year, and if we went to the expense of printing them, we would have to ask for a much more considerable sum than we are doing. Even then, I fear tlie great bulk would never be asked fox-.

Our present method discourages tlie sale of any of these copies. You have to pay $3 or $4 now to get a copy of a patent, whereas if the price were nominal there would be a great demand for these copies which does not exist now. And if you sold a few copies, that would meet the cost of (lie printing generally.
Mr, FISHER. Of course if any one wants a patent merely out of curiosity, intending to throw it away immediately after looking at it, lie will not care to pay $3 or $4. But if lie wanted it for any serious purpose, lie would consider that a very trifling expense. The officers of the department have carefully looked into the matter on several different occasions and they consider that tlie expense would be too great.

I think the hon. the minister would find that if the price were considerably reduced, there would be demand for copies which would pay for the expense of printing. My hon. friend promised to tell us about the amount he was going to ask for for tlie collection of statistics, criminal statistics, census statistics and the others to be gathered by the Department of Agriculture.

I have not been able to go into further details, and this item of $18,200 is simply a repetition of last year's vote. The Census Bill has only just passed through the House, and I have not yet been able to make careful, detailed calculations of the expenses under it. But I will try to make these calculations and be ready to give the information my bon. friend asks when I propose, as I mean to do, the supple-

meat ary vote. That vote will probably be larger than this. This a mere repetition of the vote which we had last year, and I am not now prepared to give the details the bon. gentleman asked for.
Aid to agricultural societies, $7,000.

This is required in order to give the usual aid to agricultural societies in the Northwest. I have frequently explained that, in the different provinces the provincial governments aid agricultural societies, but, there being no provincial government in the Territories, parliament has voted this sum year after year. In view of the fact that Bills for the creation of new provinces are before the House, I do not know whether this vote will be needed. But those Bills have not yet been passed, and we cannot know what the arrangement will be. I think it better to vote it this year and have it available for next fall, the time wdien the payments are made, as, 1 suppose that the provincial organization will not by that time be ready to take up this work; and certainly it will be a pity to have a cessation of the assistance to the agricultural societies.
.Mr. SPROULE. Will the minister divide it between the two provinces that are being formed?
It is paid through the secretary of agriculture for the Northwest.

How many agricultural societies are there in the Northwest ?
All'. FISHER. In 1901-5, there were thirty-one societies.
With what membership ?

I may explain that the secretary of agriculture for the Northwest supplies us each year with a list which indicates what amount should be sent to each society. Formerly it was paid on a per capita basis of membership, but lately the Department of Agriculture in the North-[DOT] west lias taken account of the money raised by the agricultural societies themselves, as well as the membership. AVe have not, for a number of years back, undertaken to decide what each society should have. That has been left to the Department of Agriculture of the Territories. They know that there is $7,000 coming, and they send us a statement and vouchers that the several societies have fulfilled the conditions, and we send a cheque to each society. I have here a list showing the membership of the societies in 1903, but not for 1904. The Regina society had a membership of 334, that being the largest society, and the smallest society had a membership of 75. They average about 150 to 200.
They would receive an average of about $225 per society?
Yes, I believe the territorial government give them some allowance also.
Is the grant from tlio Dominion paid according to the amount the society raises? Formerly the rule in Ontario was that the province paid $2 for every $1 that each agricultural society raised.

It is upon that that the territorial grant is based, and the secretary of agriculture of the Territories, when he divides the $7,000 here voted and gives us the items, takes that into consideration, I believe. In Quebec, I think it is the same as in Ontario, the assistance from the provinces varies according to the amount the society raises. That cannot be carried out in this case because the amount is fixed.
Would this vote be available if new provinces are established in the Northwest? Would the Auditor General be satisfied to pay out on such a vote as this?	.
I could not say positively as to that. This is simply an appropriation to aid agricultural societies.
In the Northwest Territories?

It does not say so. As a matter of fact it has been used only for the Northwest Territories. I think it is not likely that by the time this grant is needed, next fall, the provincial governments will be in a position to do this work, and I think it would be unfortunate if any lapse should occur and the societies should not get the usual aid.
Towards compiling historical data in regard to the Acadian families in Canada, $1,400.

I would like the Alin-ister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) to state to the committee who is compiling this historical data, how long the work has been going on. and what progress has thus far been made ?

The gentleman who is doing this work is Air. Gaudet, who was recommended to me many years ago by the gentlemen in the House of Commons and Senate, on both sides of politics, who represented constituencies in which there were a large number of Acadian residents. He was accustomed to this work ; and at that time representations were made that probably the work -would be accomplished in a few years. The period was not definitely indicated, but it was expected that the work would go on with fair rapidity. I must say frankly that I have been disappointed in the progress of the work. Air. Gaudet has collected a great mass of information, partly by travelling about in the maritime provinces, partly by a careful examination of local, municipal and other records, which

mass of information he has been working at to try and complete the first volume of his record. But almost invariably when he has reached a certain point in this work he has found other information which has delayed the final compilation, if I may call it such, or the making up of the final record ; and the result is that to-day not a single volume has been published or is finished. I have asked the archivist, Mr. Doughty, who is an expert in this kind of work, to take up this matter and go into the records which Mr. Gaudet has collected, and see if he can find means by which this work can be more rapidly and more successfully conducted. I may say that Mr. Doughty has done this to a very considerable extent; he has not examined the whole of the records yet, but he has examined them to some extent, and he finds that there is a mass of information there which will be of great value. But that information has to be carefully gone over and systematized before it can be published. Mr. Gaudet is doing that now, and I believe that within a reasonable time, with the supervision and assistance of Mr. Doughty, he will be able to complete the first volume. I may say that the information he has found is far greater than could be published in one volume, but it is so mixed up, if I may use that term, that it is impossible for him to select and pick out a portion and bring it to the condition necessary for publication. I believe, however, that with the supervision and assistance Mr. Doughty can give him, within a reasonable time he will be able to eliminate from this mass of information such portions as can be published in one volume, and then go ahead with another portion and prepare it for another volume. The mass of information he has obtained is enormous,_ and quite sufficient for several volumes, but it needs careful going over to bring it to a condition where it will be ready for publication.
Fumigating stations, $4,000.

These stations are at St. John, N.B., for the maritime provinces ; St. Johns, Que., for the province of Quebec ; Niagara Falls and Windsor, for the province of Ontario ; Winnipeg, for the province of Manitoba ; and Vancouver, for the province of British Columbia. Of course, there may be some slight importations at other ports, but these are the most important and convenient.
Exhibitions, $75,000.

This vote is for the next fiscal year, and is to cover the completion of the exhibition at Liege, Belgium, which commences about the 1st of May next, and which we have accepted an invitation to take part in ; also it is intended to continue, to a certain extent, to take part in what is called trade exhibitions in England, the first of which we took part in during last fall, and which seems to have been a Mr. FISHER.
very successful investment of money. Roughly speaking, I think that $50,000 or $60,000 of this vote will be needed to complete the Liege exhibition, and the balance will be used for the trade exhibitions in Great Britain.

How much was spent on the St. Louis exhibition altogether ?
Mr. FISHER, Up to the present time $298,000 has been spent, and I think $10,000 or $12,000 more will be required to close up all the accounts, making a total of just about $310,000.
I suppose all the goods that were sent there will be sold and deducted from that amount ?

No. A few goods were sold there, but very few. In the first place, the customs regulations are such that it is actually cheaper to bring the goods back here than to sell them there. In the next place, a very large proportion of the goods that were sent there were not of a perishable nature, and are to be utilized for the Liege exhibition and others ; they are what I may call permanent exhibition stock. I was asked this morning, and I find that in the neighbourhood of $35,000 has been spent on what we may call permanent exhibition stock. This was bought for the St. Louis exhibition, and is still available for use in other exhibitions, and I would not think of selling it. It is a stock that is far too valuable to sell. I do not want to boast, but I will say that we had at St. Louis a mineral exhibit which has not been equalled by any exhibit ever shown at any exhibition in the world. That is talking pretty big, as we say, but at the same time I have the statement of disinterested parties, Americans, well able to judge, and that is their opinion. That exhibit contained a lot of minerals that were very valuable, but which were so exceptionally good as exhibits that I felt it was in our interest to purchase them rather than to have them owned by anybody else. We had one exhibit there for which we spent about $8,000, but which we could sell to-day for much more than that. I would not think of selling it, so long as we are going to exhibit at international exhibitions. There were other exhibits of timber, fur, &e., that cost considerable sums of money, but which attracted great attention, and which it would be very hard to replace. The money value of these is not so great as the expense of collection. We have had to send men all over the country to collect them, and the cost of collection was more than the cost of the exhibits. We own these now, and in the future will not have to go to the expense of collecting ; this will enable us to put up an excellent exhibit at Liege at less cost.

I had not the pleasure of being at the St. Louis exhibition, but I inquired from gentlemen who were there and

they congratulated us on our fine exhibit. With reference to this exhibit in Belgium, is it the intention of the government to have an exhibit somewhat similar to the Glasgow exhibit of is it to be larger or smaller ?

The cost will be more ; it is a larger exhibition than the Glasgow exhibition. We are going to have a Canadian building with all our exhibits in the one building, and this costs more than to have space in each of the buildings, but we have found by experience that it is far more effective. It saves a little in cost of administration but in effectiveness there is no comparison. At Liege we have to pay a rent for the land on which our building will be placed, half a dollar a foot, amounting in all to about $7,000. The contract price for the building is about $33,000. It is a large item and when I first got the estimate I shrank from it, but when I came to examine the alternative of obtaining space in the different buildings and the difference in the cost of administration and management, I came to the conclusion that even at that expense, if we were going to exhibit at all, it was best to undertake that expenditure. The estimate to-day is that the LiSge exhibition will cost from $120,000 to $125,000. Judging from my experience we will be able to keep within that. I estimated that our expenditure at St. Louis would be about $300,000 ; it is going to cost about $310,000, so I think I was fairly accurate in that estimate. The Glasgow exhibit cost about $70,000 or $75,000.
Mr. .1. D. REID. I agree that if you are having an exhibit of any kind which is for the purpose of advertising our country you should have a good one, because otherwise the money would be entirely thrown away. T understood that the expense of this was to be about $75,000.

The $50,000 is to be expended after the 1st of July. All the expense of preparing the exhibits, sending them over, erecting the building and all ether expenses up to the 1st of July is paid out of this year's vote, the $200,000 we had this year.
What amount has been spent on the Li6ge exhibition?

I am told that up to the present time, although I have not the exact figures, we have spent about $25,000 or $30,000. We have not yet sent a cheque for the buildings, but we will have to do so in a few weeks.
I). REID. Is not half a dollar a foot rather a heavy rental ?

We have a permanent exhibition commissioner, now in the department, who has been in the department for about four years, Mr. William Hutchison. We will have to appoint another commissioner for the I.iege exhibition, because Mr. Hutchison does not understand French,
I). REID. Will Mr. Hutchison be there too ?

Oh, yes, he is the business commissioner, who will attend to the administration and will certainly have to be there. If he understood French it probably would not be necessary for me to appoint anybody else, but under the circumstances I would not like to put the business work of the exhibition under the management of an inexperienced person. I believe that the success of our exhibitions lately has been very largely due to the fact that we have at the head of that department, Mr. Hutchison, who for three or four years has had great experience in exhibition work.
Is he a permanent employee, and if so, at what salary ?
He is permanent at $3,000 a year.

And expenses ?
Mr. FISHER Yes, when they are incurred.
Will the minister give us a further explanation as to these exhibitions in England ; do I understand that he expects to make them permanent.

My hon. friend misunderstood me if he thought I said they would be permanent. In England there are held annually what are known as trade exhibitions; at the Islington Agricultural Hall in London there are held five or six of these each year. Last fall there were three which came within a week of each other, each lasting ten days. One was the exhibition of the grocers and allied trades ; another, the bakers, and another a dairying exhibition. We had been for several years invited to take part in these exhibitions but for one reason or another we had been unable to do so. My officers and I were impressed with the value to Canadian trade of our taking part in these exhibitions which are attended by the retail and wholesale merchants from all over the country, who pick up new ideas in any of the trades in which they are specially interested. We took part in these three exhibitions last fall.
What was the cost ?
That is not an unreasonable charge for space in exhibitions of this kind. Sometimes they charge as much as a dollar a foot.
Who is the commissioner ?

The cost amounted to about $5,000 each. There was another exhibition of a somewhat similar character called the Colonial Products exhibition held in 'St. Georges Hall. Liverpool, and we also took part in that at an expense of $5,000

or $0,000. The trade journals of the old country have universally congratulated us on having shown Canadian products at these exhibitions, and our experience is that our exhibits have caused a good deal of stir among the trades interested. X believe this work is of the utmost value to us in pushing our agriculture and food products in the English markets. So far as my opinion is concerned, I believe we should take part another year in some of these exhibitions, though not necessarily in the same ones as last year. An expenditure of $15,000 or $20,000 in such work is of the greatest value to Canadian trade in the English market.
Did the $15,000 for the three exhibitions cover the cost of collecting the exhibits and forwarding them to England?
Yes.
Did you have to get new exhibits for each exhibition?

No. Part of the exhibits could be shown at the three exhibitions. At the grocers' exhibition we had canned goods, bacon, pork, and some butter and cheese ; at the dairy exhibition we had butter and cheese, eggs, and dressed poultry; at the baker's exhibit, we had butter and lard, some canned goods, flour, breakfast foods and articles of that kind. At these exhibitions, of late years we have set out the exhibits in an attractive and striking way which might perhaps be called a trick of the trade; something like what shop keepers do in what is called window dressing. At these three exhibitions in London we used these same decorations, although the exhibits themselves were changed. I am glad to say that I have some officers in my department who are experts at displaying our goods ; and when presented in this manner the exhibits attracted a good deal of attention.
You will only have to renew the expense once a year ?

If the three exhibitions were held in the same hall, yes. But In the change from London to Liverpool, we had to renew the decorations. A good deal of this decoration is of grasses and grains which are very effective and very beautiful, and these we have to renew from time to time.
Who had charge of the London exhibit?

Mr. Hay and Mr. Brodie; the latter gentleman speaks French very well and he has gone to Lifge. Mr. Race showed great aptitude at St. Louis, and I got him to go to Liverpool; he is not a permanent officer.
Are these the only exhibitions we are to take part in during the coming year?

The Liege exhibition and these trade exhibitions in London are the only ones provided for in this vote, and the only ones we have so far considered.
For renewing and improving Canadian exhibits at Imperial Institute, London, and assisting in the maintenance thereof, $8,000.
What changes have taken place in this office ?
What is this city office for ?

It is for two purposes. In the first place there has been a constant objection that the Imperial Institute was too far in the west end to be convenient for business men. In connection with The city office there is a show room, where I hope to have brief temporary exhibits. For instance, one week eve may have an exhibit of canned goods, another week bacon and pork, another week something else ; and each exhibit will be advertised beforehand to the trade specially interested in the particular line of products exhibited. The exhibits in the city will be exhibits of goods of a perishable nature, lasting only a few days or a week, whereas the exhibition at the Imperial Institute at South Kensington is one of a more permanent and general character. At the city office we might have in the course of the year fifteen or twenty different exhibits.
The office will be run the whole year round ?
Yes.
Then you will require a permanent officer ?
Yes.
The amount is scarcely sufficient to carry such an enterprise in the city and do it effectively.

We expect that Mr. Watson, with an ordinary clerk, will he able to alternate between the exhibit at South Kensingtou and the office in the city. When the exhibit is going on he will spend most of his time there and have his clerk at the South Kensington Institute.
Does he give all his time to this work for the sum of $1,500 a year ?
Yes, he does nothing else. He only got $1,200 for a long time.

Can you get a good officer for that price ?
. Mr. FISHER. I am surprised that Mr. Watson is contented, but he is an efficient officer. He has been there a long time, and is well up in Canadian products and affairs, and a most suitable man for the purpose.
He is a very line man.
I cannot see why he is willing to go on at the low price, but he is.
He is a very efficient gentleman, and I am surprised at the smallness of his salary. He must have some private income.
I know nothing about that.
What inducements are held out to manufacturers to exhibit ? Have they to pay their own freight, or what means should they take to have their goods exhibited ?

I have not made out any special rules regarding this exhibition. In preparing exhibits, if the manufacturers will supply the goods, we have always been in the habit of sending them forward at our expense and looking after them. I suppose we will have to do that in connection with the Imperial Institute exhibit.
The hon. gentleman is referring to exhibitions, not to the Imperial Institute.
We will do the same in that case.

I think the hon. gentleman has been a negligent sinner once more. He has not carried out what he promised last session and the session before that, and has not much of an excuse to offer.
Mr. FISHER, I have not got on as fast as I would like.
In what condition is the Canadian exhibit in the Imperial Institute at the present time, and how is it constituted ?
I do not know if I could tell the hon. gentleman.
The hon. gentleman is ashamed of it.
I do not want to say much about it.
Is it increasing or decreasing ?
It is very much in statu quo at present, but before next July, I hope to be able to increase it very considerably.
It is not a credit to the country, that exhibition in the Imperial Institute.
What is the use of spending $8,000 if we make no efforts to improve it ?

We did not spend it last year at all, but I hope that by the end of this year we will be able to make the exhibit fairly creditable. I may not succeed in doing all I would like before the 1st July, but will make a decided effort.
What do you propose doing ?

I propose to collect exhibits this year as much as I can with the money at my disposal, and send them over and set them up. Once the installation at Li^ge is completed. I hope to turn some of the staff back into London to do the installation there. The Liege exhibition must be installed by the 1st May, and I will have May and June to work in the Imperial Institute at London.
Steamer service at Grosse Isle, $55,000.

The amount of the contract is $83,000 for the vessel, and it will take the vote of last year of $30,000 and this year's $55,000 to pay for it. When I asked for $30,000 last year, I did not know what the contract would come to. We invited tenders from a considerable number of builders, and eventually awarded the contract to the lowest Canadian tenderer. There were tenders from abroad at a lower price, but we thought it only fair to give a chance to Canadian builders. Bertram & Company, of Toronto, are the contractors.
When will the contract be finished ?

The vessel is to be delivered in September. There were other tenders that ran up to $110,000, and ffie tender we accepted was the lowest Canadian tender. It will be an iron steamer 120 feet long and otherwise in proportion.

1S40
I presume you expect to spend this $30,000 voted last year before the 30th June next, and the balance Is to pay for the rest of the contract ?
Yes.

$80,000 seems a high figure for a vessel 120 feet long.
v Mr. FISHER. We asked for tenders from some four or five builders in Canada and two in Scotland. The offers from Scotland were lower, but we thought it would be fair to add 25 per cent to them to account for the duty which the Canadian builders said they had to pay on the material. When we did that, the Scotch tenders came higher than $83,000. The 25 per cent is an arbitrary figure, but it is about what the average duty would be, and I thought it best to give the contract to a Canadian builder on reasonable terms.

I understand that, of late, they have been building large steel steamers in Toronto for prices quite as low as are demanded in the old country. Had the minister made inquiries he would have learned that a large number of lake vessels have been built in Toronto. Therefore, if he has added 25 per cent, he has simply given a profit of 25 per cent or $20,000 to the builders over and above what the vessel could have been built for if the contract had been by tender.

It was by tender, and none of the tenders were opened until all were in. There was one Scotch tender for $67,000, another for $73,000 ? The Bertram tender was for $83,000 and the Collingwood Ship-building Company and the Poisons each $110,000.
On the same specifications?
The same in every way.
Is it understood that there are to be no extras?

There would have to be a change in the specifications to have extras. The specifications were prepared by the Department of Marine and Fisheries just as they prepare them for themselves when they have to order a boat. Of course, the officers of my department explained the work to be done by the boat and what she would need.

The minister has taken a novel way of introducing the protection principle when he says that he added 25 per cent to the Scotch tender. It seems a strange way to overcome a protective duty in the interest of Canadians. I am not objecting to it but I think it is a very bad principle to introduce.
I think it is the principle that lias been acted upon by the government in a great many instances.
I do not remember having heard it explained or defended in the House before.
When the matter was discussed, I was informed that the Public Works Department act on this principle.
In connection with what work?
I cannot say; I was simply told they acted on the principle of adding a percentage to the tender of the transAtlantic contractor, so as to make it as fair as possible for our own contractor.

I have heard it explained that it cost something to bring a vessel across the water, and that must be taken into the calculation in comparing tenders. But I cannot remember having ever heard of the addition of a percentage to the tender from outside of Canada in order to be fair to our contractors.

The Minister of Agriculture does not appear to be as economical as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Pr&fontaine). I think that when that lion, gentleman wants a steamer he purchases it, on the other side of the water. Is it not true that the government purchased a steamer last year, ordering it from the other side of the Atlantic on the ground that it could lie built there at a less price than here?
I think the reason was that they could not get it delivered here in time. I might say that these tenders from the other side of the water were for a vessel delivered at Quebec.

That is why I made the inquiry-because I understood that the cost of delivering the vessel on this side was the only item in the calculation in considering Canadian tenders. Now, it is put on the ground of protection. This is an illustration that devised many means to introduce the element of protection, though they would not admit the principle openly. They have accomplished it in a round-about way in many instances, of which this is one.
Has the minister named the vessel? I think we should decide on a name. I think we ought to call her the ' Minnie M.'
I do not know that name?
What speed will the vessel have ?
The specifications require 12 knots.
The vessel is for quarantine purposes. Will she carry passengers?

We have constantly to send numbers of .people from the quarantine station at Grosse Isle to Quebec-people

whose time of quarantine has expired- when there is no vessel to carry them. The vessel has to carry also a disinfecting apparatus, so that if a ship comes that requires disinfecting that can be done.
Has the department any different method for disinfecting ships from that which was in use some years ago 1

I do not know of any change within the last seven years. This vessel will have what they call the sulphur blast furnace.
Sieamer for service at William Head, $20,000.
I have not been able to make a contract for that ship yet. Specifications are now being drawn up by the Department of Marine and Fisheries I hope to get the ship built on the Pacific coast.
What is the object of this vessel ?
This vessel belongs to the quarantine station 'at Victoria. We have to have a small steamer there to run out to the ships as they come in, and take off passengers if necessary.
Have you any reason to hope that you will be able to get this built in British Columbia ?
Yes.
Specifications were prepared last year, what is the cause of the delay ?
Specifications were prepared, but they were on too extensive a scale, too large a ship altogether, and I insisted upon having specifications for a smaller vessel.
What are you doing the service with now ?

An old boat which has been under constant repair, costing us very heavily every year, and which is not fit for the service. Sometimes I almost wish that she might be lost, she is absolutely unfit for service.
Salaries and contingencies of organized districts. and public health in other districts, $150,000.

I would like to ask the .minister for some information regarding some unsettled claims in the town of Pin-cher Creek where 1 live. Three or four years ago there was a small pox epidemic in the Northwest Territories, and it broke out in that town. The Northwest government took steps to prevent the spread of the disease, they appointed health officers and a committee to look after the matter. They quarantined several houses in the town, and held people occupying them under quaran-t ne. When the time came to settle, the Northwest government had not sufficient funds to meet all the claims, because there
\\ ere other cases in other towns. I understand that an agreement was arrived at between the Dominion government and the government of the Northwest Territories, and the cases were handed over to the Department of Agriculture. In some of the towns in my district the claims were settled in their entirety, but for some reason of which I am not aware, in other places they were not satisfied. There are two towns in the district which I represent, where not < ver twenty-five or thirty per cent of all the claims have been settled, though they were certified to by the health officer, or the health committee appointed by the Northwest government, and sworn statements were submitted. I would like to ask the minister if he can tell me why these claims have not been paid ? I think they should be paid, it is in the interest of the country that they should be paid.

I may say to my hon. friend that I do not quite understand the situation as he has described it. I was not aware that the Northwest government had any health officers there apart from those we appoint and pay. But the hon. gentleman seems to indicate some local or other health officers. As a matter of fact, we had to deal with the small-pox epidemic in the Northwest, and we did so through Dr. Patterson, who was appointed by us to superintend this work in the Territories. Everything the hon. gentleman describes came before Dr. Patterson, and he made reports upon it to the department, passed the various claims and so forth, and wherever he passed claims we paid them. I do not remember at the moment any cases which were not settled, though in some cases we did not pay the full amount claimed, but in those cases the matter was amicably adjusted. I am not aware that there were any outstanding claims. If my hon. friend would give the names of the places and the individuals whose claims remain unsettled, I will be glad to look into them, if they are certified and approved by the officer in charge.

The Dr. Patterson to whom the minister refers did make a visit to this town in order to settle these claims. He came there and spoke to one or two men of the town, I do not think there were three men who knew of his business in the town, although there were over twenty interested in these claims. When lie came at noon he said lie would be there the whole afternoon, and he went away in an hour or two, and never made any investigation of the claims, good, bad or indifferent. I was there, and am able to make this statement. He put his own interpretation upon our claims, and they have not been settled to this day. I iiope the minister will look into this matter and set it right. I can give all the details, the names of the applicants, and everything necessary to justify my statement. I am now speaking of Pinclier Creek, but I

believe there were similar claims unpaid at Fort Macleod. This occurred four years ago last February. The disease broke out in Pinc-her Creek about the same time. I know of one instance where the officers took possession of a vacant house, placed patients in same, also furniture and bedding, and it all remains in that house up to this time. The board of health recommended that the building should be burned down, but no action has yet been taken.
I will look into the matter and see what has been done.

The hon. gentleman has a number of officers to guard the frontier in Manitoba from contagious diseases. Has the minister appointed any new officers during the past year? He had Dr. Riddell at Crystal City, Dr. Thorburn at Deloraine, and Dr. White from some other place down there.
No, we have taken them all off. Small-pox seems to have practically disappeared from the United States and we have felt justified in withdrawing these officers.
Small-pox is the only disease that you guard against?
Yes.
How many officers have you appointed for the unorganized districts and what are their salaries?

Those along the frontier are appointed from month to month and are paid $100 a month except a few in the west where the expenses are higher and where they are paid $125 a month, as they are not resident at the places at which they are stationed.
If you have dispensed with the services of so many medical men and do not intend to employ them again, except an emergency arises, why do you want this large vote?

I do not now expect to need all that, but at the time these estimates were made up, two or three months ago, we could not be very sure. We may be able to get on with $20,000 or $25,000 less and I would be willing to reduce the vote by $20,-
000.
How much did you spend last year ?

The Auditor General's Report will show what we spent last year; I am speaking now of the current year. I do not think we will spend $150,000 this present year, because the necessity for watching the frontier has ceased during this current fiscal year, and if nothing occurs to require the reappointment of these men during the next four or five years we will not spend the $150,000.

The Auditor General's Report shows that last year $106,216 was spent, $73,056.60 for the organized districts and $33,159.40 for the unorganized districts, for public health generally. The minister states that he will not require $20,000 of last year's expenditure this year, so that about $83,000 should cover the expenditure for this year.
Of course the organized districts are all we can surely count on. The other work is intermittent in its character, but we never know exactly what we will be called upon to spend.
Last year $73,000 was for the organized districts and $33,000 for the unorganized districts. The hon. minister does not mean to say that that will be increased at all.
There must be some mistake there, because last year I think we spent nearly $150,000; otherwise I would not have asked for the $150,000.
There must be some other portion of the Auditor General's Report which my hon. friend has not seen.

Some years ago, I asked for $80,000 for the organized districts alone, but I was forced to take a supplementary-estimate and I think it came to $100,000 altogether. That has been the expenditure generally.

You should not take a larger vote than is required for this purpose, because there is great temptation to use the money for some other purpose. The Auditor General has complained in respect to matters of this kind.
I do not want the temptation of getting more money than I actually need.
Then why do you not act on that principle?

The minister says that this year he does not want within $20,000 of wliat he expended last year. He spent $106,000 last year and $20,000 less would be $86,000. If he gets $100,000 it ought to cover all reqtiirements.

In the year 1902-3, we expended on the organized districts alone $99,000, so that there appears to be something omitted in the Auditor General's Report. I am perfectly willing to let the item stand until I get further information, but if the hon. gentlemen wish to pass the vote I think it might be reduced to $130,000.
You must have had some memorandum to present to Council on which to base your request for this vote.
I have not that memorandum with me at present.
The expenditure last year according to the Auditor General's Report was $217,000, and if you deduct the $99,000 for cattle quarantine it leaves a balance of $118,000 expended in this way.
The estimate for 1905-G shows $105,000 for organized quarantine work; $15,000 for frontier work, and $10,000 for Northwest Territories, or $130,000 in all.
The minister had better let the item stand until we get the information.

Very well.
Item allowed to stand.
Traeadie Lazaretto, $6,000.
Mr, SPROULE. Why is this vote increased $500?

The physician there is experimenting on a new treatment and he wishes to continue his experiments more extensively. That accounts for the larger part of the increase, and then there are some little travelling expenses which the doctor has to incur in examining into reported cases of leprosy.
Are the lepers increasing?

It varies a little. There are seventeen now and two years ago there were twenty-one.
Public Works Health Act, $6,000.

The statute passed some years ago requires that certain facilities in the matter of hospital accommodation and so on, shall be provided by contractors on public works. We have a gentleman who visits these works and sees that this law is properly carried out.
Mr. .1. D. REID. I see that last year the expenditure under this head was only $3,500.

I asked for the vote of $6,000 last year in anticip'ation of the construction of the Transcontinental Railway. So far we have only expended about $3,000, but before the end of the current fiscal year we may have to expend more. So far, I am very pleased to say, there has been no unusual occurrence. The ordinary routine inspection has been sufficient. We have had very little in the way of complaint, and our inspector has been able, by ordinary travelling, to overlook the work and make satisfactory reports. As an instance of what might occur at any time, a report came to the department that there was an epidemic of a peculiar disease on a certain work. The inspector immediately went off to inquire into it, and returned within a week with the statement that there was no foundation for the report. When a report of that kind comes to the department, however, we look into it at once.
Winnipeg and St. Boniface hospitals, $4,000.
How are the grants to these hospitals made ?
The vote is divided between them according to the number of patients, at the rate of so much per day.

It was stated in this House a year or two ago that the reason we had to give so much to hospitals in that part of the country was that a large number of immigrants were taken to them, and it would be unfair to throw the whole burden upon the people there. Will the minister state how many are in the hospitals, and what proportion are immigrants ?

I have no report of the number there at present, and I do not think that would influence the grant. It is the number of admissions of newly arrived people during the year that regulates the amount we send to each hospital.
